comment: CBI67 records why the host stopped a provider and makes the cause CBI51 reads issuer-controlled. A vector states what the store holds for one occurrence and pins the attribution it issues. The store needs no provider process, so these vectors are pure data; that CBI51 acts on the issued cause is pinned separately by the restart scenarios, which do run real providers.

vectors.name: an-availability-stop-is-attributed-and-restartable
vectors.comment: The ordinary path. CBI50's enforcement recorded the stop after terminating the provider, and the cause it wrote is the one CBI51 reads.

vectors.name: a-trust-withdrawal-is-attributed-and-refused
vectors.comment: CBI46's sweep recorded the stop. This refusal was already double-guarded by CBI51's own authorization check, so the record adds attribution rather than safety here.

vectors.name: an-operator-retirement-is-attributed-and-refused
vectors.comment: The case this slice exists for. A publisher that is still trusted passes every other check, so before the record a caller claiming availability about a deliberately retired provider got a restart the policy would have denied.

vectors.name: no-record-is-an-unexpected-exit
vectors.comment: Every stop the host performs writes a record, so absence means the host did not stop it. That is the honest reading and also the restartable one.

vectors.name: a-record-for-another-deployment-is-stale
vectors.comment: The store holds a record for this occurrence under a staged identity it is no longer running. That describes a different deployment, and a host holding a record it cannot match does not guess either way.
